items.full: WooCommerce is the open-source ecommerce platform for WordPress. Our core platform is free, flexible, and amplified by a global community. The freedom of open-source means you retain full ownership of your store’s content and data forever. Whether you’re launching a business, taking brick-and-mortar retail online, or developing sites for clients, use WooCommerce for a store that powerfully blends content and commerce. Built-in tools and popular integrations help you efficiently manage your business operations. Many services are free to add with a single click via the optional Setup Wizard . WooCommerce means business. Keep tabs on the performance metrics most important to you with a powerful and flexible central dashboard built into WooCommerce. Expand your audience across marketing and social channels with Google Ads , HubSpot , Mailchimp , and Facebook integrations. You can always check out the in-dashboard Marketing Hub for fresh ideas and tips to help you succeed. Developers can use WooCommerce to create, customize, and scale a store to meet a client’s exact specifications, making enhancements through extensions or custom solutions. The core platform is tested rigorously and often, supported by a dedicated development team working across time zones. Comprehensive documentation is updated with each release, empowering you to build exactly the store required. WooCommerce has a large, passionate community dedicated to helping merchants succeed – and it’s growing fast. There are WooCommerce Meetups in locations around the world that you can attend for free and even get involved in running. These events are a great way to learn from others, share your expertise, and connect with like-minded folks. WooCommerce also has a regular presence at WordCamps across the globe – we’d love to meet you. WooCommerce is developed and supported by Automattic, the creators of WordPress.com and Jetpack. We also have hundreds of independent contributors, and there’s always room for more. Head to the WooCommerce GitHub Repository to find out how you can pitch in. items.title: Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027
items.desc: Starting in 2027, Google plans to turn off AI features in its school products by default, letting schools decide what to enable. The catch: schools that block AI entirely on their devices will also lose access to Google Search, since the two systems are now too deeply intertwined to separate. Given Google's grip on the US school market, that "choice" doesn't leave schools with much room to maneuver. The article Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027 appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Starting in early 2027, Google will give schools an ultimatum: accept AI for students or lose access to Google Search entirely. Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will all be off by default for student accounts. Schools can turn each one on individually. But a version of search without AI? That's no longer on the table. The New York Times broke the story first. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, said search and AI have become too tightly fused to pull apart. Google recently flipped AI features on by default inside its learning platform Classroom for schools with Gemini access. That move drew backlash, and the company is now reversing course. Schools that choose to enable search will get two flavors: search with full AI overviews and AI chat, or search with "Guided Learning," a mode designed to steer students toward answers rather than hand them over directly. None of this happens in a vacuum. Google dominates the US school market with Chromebooks, Gmail, and Classroom. Education professor Morgan Polikoff called the move a textbook case of the tech industry shoving AI onto people whether they want it or not. The country's two largest school districts, New York City and Los Angeles, had already pulled back on AI for students in September. Los Angeles specifically wanted to keep using Google Search without AI overviews. Google won't let them. items.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
items.desc: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.
items.full: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images AI Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity Russell Brandom 2:41 PM PST · November 3, 2026 Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . items.title: Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS
items.desc: Combining :nth-child with style queries and sibling-index() to conditionally select child elements. Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. The title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly. Let’s suppose you have the following: div:nth-child(5n + 8) { background: red; } And you decide to update the 5 or the 8 . The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want: .container { --A: 5; --B: 8; } .container > div:nth-child(var(--A)*n + var(--B)) { background: red; } With my implementation, you will be able to do it! The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way. We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of
elements inside it.
And the container controls the variables of :nth-child() : .container { --A: ; --B: ; } .container > div { /* based on the values of --A and --B change the background value */ background: ??; } I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow. :nth-child(B) Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element: div:nth-child(5) { } I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected. We can translate this into the following CSS code: .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); } Is this a valid CSS code?! Yes, it’s valid, and it works! I am using the new if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style() . If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens. We can also have an if/else : .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue); } CodePen Embed Fallback The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows: .container div { background: if(style( condition ): ; else: ); } The tricky part is how to define the condition within style() . I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if() .” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid: .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); background: if(style(sibling-index() = var(--B)): red); background: if(style(var(--B) = sibling-index()): red); background: if(style(--B = sibling-index()): red); } We have our first implementation! ChatGPT can now turn text prompts and photos into animated GIFs with OpenAI's Images 2.6 model
items.desc: OpenAI is adding a GIF feature to ChatGPT. With the new Images 2.6 model, users can create animated GIFs from text prompts or photos and then adjust speed and individual frames. The model's image consistency is strong enough to keep characters recognizable across frames, making flipbook-style animation possible. According to OpenAI, users now generate more than four billion images per week. The article ChatGPT can now turn text prompts and photos into animated GIFs with OpenAI's Images 2.6 model appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: ChatGPT can now create animated GIFs. The update is based on OpenAI's new Images 2.6 model and is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on web, desktop, and mobile apps, The Verge reports. Users can generate a GIF from a text prompt or uploaded photo, then adjust animation speed or edit individual frames. As an example, OpenAI showed how the prompt "Can you make a gif of a cat dancing?" produces several slight variations of a character that are strung together flipbook-style into a GIF. The model's image consistency appears strong enough to keep the character recognizable across frames, while earlier models would likely have altered its look too much from one frame to the next for the trick to work. Beyond GIFs, Images 2.6 is also meant to speed up image generation overall. For developers, OpenAI is also releasing the API models GPT-Image-2.6 "Flare" for efficient and "Sunburst" for higher-quality image generation. Both model variants were first introduced with Image 2.5 . OpeneAI says users now generate well over four billion images per week via ChatGPT and the API, one billion more than in September. items.title: PCrisk Trust Badge Review: A Verifiable Security Badge for WordPress
items.desc: High-reputation websites need to display trust credentials. My PCrisk Trust Badge review covers a solution that helps you achieve this with ease through displaying a dynamic (and customizable) badge. The post " PCrisk Trust Badge Review: A Verifiable Security Badge for WordPress " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: Any website that relies on trust to facilitate sales needs to showcase that wherever customers show up. I’ve got a PCrisk Trust Badge review today that gives you a near-perfect solution! It makes regular scans of your site for malware and other malicious intent, then displays a badge if all is well. However, if something comes up in the scan, the badge will hide again until you resolve it. The premise is simple, but this review will help you decide whether its application is also straightforward. Spoiler alert: I think it’s an easy decision to make! I’ll start with the three premium plans and give you the lowdown on the free version after. Note that the prices here are for month-by-month billing and annual plans come with two months free usage: As for the free version, PCrisk will scan one site, once per month, then sends you the results complete with a trust score and summary. None of the premium functionality is available in the free version. I’m going to talk more about the use cases shortly. However, in short, the Solo plan is ideal for a single store. If you run an agency, Pro would suit you. The Business plan would also work for an agency with a larger portfolio, or if you know that portfolio will grow in the future. PCrisk Trust Badge is also available as a Shopify app and as a script snippet for any other website platform, but the focus is (of course) on the WordPress plugin for this review. WordPress security plugins do a huge service to millions of sites. In my opinion, they’re likely the hardest working plugins you’ll install. However, the public never sees any of this. In some cases, the website will display a static seal or badge to indicate that the site has security. PCrisk Trust Badge displays a dynamic badge. This links to a public report that shows details such as the scan date, a trust score, and the engines it used. If a scan fails, the badge won’t show. The scan itself covers a few areas: Malware, phishing feeds, obfuscated scripts, SSL validity, and more. However, your current WordPress security plugin still has a vital part to play as PCrisk Trust Badge only detects and reports on issues. Agency owners will love the peace of mind this gives to clients. In fact, anyone who runs multiple sites will find value in the plugin. So will WooCommerce stores, small businesses or lead-generation websites. Anywhere customers need to know your site is safe to pass their data through will find benefits in PCrisk Trust Badge. The core of PCrisk Trust Badge is its scanning: daily for premium plans and monthly for the free plan. Scans run on PCrisk’s servers, so there’s no load on your site. There’s no impact on page speeds for the free version as the plugin adds nothing to public pages. It’s worth noting that PCrisk Trust Badge aims to respect data privacy. It’s a ‘cookie-free’ solution, although it does load an external script and contacts PCrisk servers. However, you have to explicitly approve those connections with WordPress. Visitors won’t see a different experience than usual, but requests do send an IP address and the page URL to PCrisk. The dynamic badge is a unique element. Building Modern HTML Emails with Rémi Parmentier As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology. I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you. Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration. It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here : It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more. “Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude , ChatGPT , GitHub Copilot , Gemini , America.gov , Glean , and other similar websites and web apps: The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps . This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri . Immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible. There is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines . They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier. I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs. Built environments also extend to digital experiences , and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established: It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.
